formulas.name: Power rule for derivatives

variables.name: gradient of xⁿ
variables.description: The derivative of xⁿ at the point x: the slope of the tangent there.

variables.name: exponent
variables.description: Any real power (whole, negative or fractional).

formulas.explanation: To differentiate a power of x, bring the power down in front and reduce the power by one. It works for every real exponent: x² gives 2x, 1/x = x⁻¹ gives -x⁻², and √x = x^(1/2) gives 1/(2√x). Combined with the rules for sums and constant multiples it differentiates every polynomial.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to differentiate polynomials and powers of x, for gradients of curves, tangents, and maxima and minima.
assumptions: x > 0 when n is not a whole number

example.story: What is the gradient of the curve y = x³ at x = 2?

formulas.name: Product rule

variables.name: value of v
variables.description: The second factor at the point.

variables.name: value of u
variables.description: The first factor at the point.

formulas.explanation: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. If u changes a little, the product changes by (change in u) × v; if v changes, by u × (change in v). Adding both effects gives u'v + uv'. Here the rule is written with numbers: the values and derivatives of u and v at one point.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to differentiate a product of two functions, such as x² sin x or x eˣ.
assumptions: u and v are differentiable at the point

example.story: Find the gradient of y = x² ln x at x = 2. Here u = x² gives u = 4 and u' = 4; v = ln x gives v ≈ 0.693147 and v' = 0.5.

formulas.name: Quotient rule

variables.name: value of v
variables.description: The denominator at the point (not zero).

formulas.explanation: Write u/v as u × v⁻¹ and use the product and chain rules: the result simplifies to (u'v - uv')/v². The order in the numerator matters because of the minus sign; a common memory aid is low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to differentiate a fraction of two functions, such as tan x = sin x / cos x or (x + 1)/(x - 1).

example.story: Find the gradient of y = x / (x + 1) at x = 1. Here u = 1, u' = 1, v = 2 and v' = 1.

formulas.name: Chain rule

variables.name: dy/dx
variables.description: Rate of change of y with respect to x.

variables.name: dy/du
variables.description: Rate of change of the outer function with respect to its input u.

variables.name: du/dx
variables.description: Rate of change of the inner function u with respect to x.

formulas.explanation: For a function inside a function, y = f(u) with u = g(x), the rates of change multiply. If u changes 3 times as fast as x, and y changes 2 times as fast as u, then y changes 6 times as fast as x. In practice: differentiate the outside, keep the inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever one function is nested inside another: sin(3x), (2x + 1)⁵, e^(x²), √(1 + x²).

example.story: Find the gradient of y = sin(3x) at x = 0.2. Here u = 3x = 0.6, so dy/du = cos 0.6 ≈ 0.825336 and du/dx = 3.

formulas.name: Derivative of an exponential

variables.name: gradient
variables.description: The derivative of e^(kx) at x.

variables.name: constant
variables.description: The multiplier of x in the exponent.

formulas.explanation: eˣ is the special function that is its own derivative: its slope at every point equals its height. With the chain rule, e^(kx) has derivative k e^(kx). This is why exponential growth means the growth rate is proportional to the amount.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for growth and decay models, and whenever e appears with x in the exponent.

example.story: Find the gradient of y = e^(0.5x) at x = 2.

formulas.name: Derivative of a sine

variables.name: gradient
variables.description: The derivative of sin(kx) at x.

variables.name: constant
variables.description: The multiplier of x inside the sine.

variables.name: point
variables.description: Where the gradient is taken, in radians.

formulas.explanation: The slope of the sine curve at any point is the cosine at that point, as long as x is in radians. A factor k inside stretches the wave horizontally and, by the chain rule, multiplies the slope by k. Similarly cos(kx) has derivative -k sin(kx).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for oscillations, waves and alternating currents, for example to get velocity from a sinusoidal displacement.

example.story: Find the gradient of y = sin(2x) at x = 0.5.

formulas.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus

variables.name: definite integral
variables.description: The signed area under f between a and b.

variables.name: antiderivative at b
variables.description: F(b), where F is any function with F' = f.

formulas.explanation: Integration and differentiation undo each other. To find the area under f from a to b, find any antiderivative F (a function whose derivative is f) and subtract its values at the ends. The constant of integration cancels, so any antiderivative works.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to evaluate every definite integral that has a known antiderivative: areas, distances from velocities, work from forces.

example.story: Evaluate the integral of 2x from 1 to 3, using the antiderivative F(x) = x².

formulas.name: Definite integral of a power

variables.name: integral
variables.description: Area under y = xⁿ from a to b.

variables.name: exponent
variables.description: The power of x, any real number except -1.

formulas.explanation: The antiderivative of xⁿ is x^(n+1)/(n+1): raise the power by one and divide by the new power. That is the power rule run backwards. Evaluating it at b and a gives the definite integral. The case n = -1 is special and gives a logarithm instead.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to integrate polynomials term by term and to find areas under power curves.
assumptions: a, b > 0 if n is not a whole number

example.story: Find the area under y = x³ between x = 0 and x = 2.

formulas.name: Definite integral of an exponential

variables.name: integral
variables.description: Area under y = e^(kx) from a to b.

variables.name: constant
variables.description: The multiplier in the exponent (not zero).

formulas.explanation: Because e^(kx) differentiates to k e^(kx), its antiderivative is e^(kx)/k. Evaluate at both limits and subtract.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for total growth over a time interval, charge flowing in an RC circuit, or areas under exponential curves.

example.story: Find the integral of e^(2x) from x = 0 to x = 1.

formulas.name: Definite integral of 1/x

variables.name: integral
variables.description: Area under y = 1/x from a to b.

formulas.explanation: The power rule for integrals fails for x⁻¹ because it would divide by zero. Instead, the antiderivative of 1/x is ln x, so the area from a to b is ln b - ln a = ln(b/a). The area depends only on the ratio b/a.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for integrals of 1/x, isothermal gas work, and the time constants of first-order processes.
assumptions: a and b have the same sign (here both positive)

example.story: Find the area under y = 1/x between x = 2 and x = 8.

formulas.name: Definite integral of a sine

variables.name: integral
variables.description: Signed area under y = sin(kx) from a to b.

formulas.explanation: The antiderivative of sin(kx) is -cos(kx)/k, because the derivative of cos is -sin. Evaluating from a to b gives (cos ka - cos kb)/k. Over a full period the positive and negative areas cancel to zero.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for areas under sine curves and for averages of oscillating quantities.

example.story: Find the area under one arch of y = sin x, from 0 to π.

formulas.name: Definite integral of a cosine

variables.name: integral
variables.description: Signed area under y = cos(kx) from a to b.

formulas.explanation: The antiderivative of cos(kx) is sin(kx)/k, since sin differentiates to cos and the chain rule brings out a factor k. Subtract the values at the two limits.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for areas under cosine curves and in Fourier and wave problems.

example.story: Find the integral of cos(2x) from 0 to π/4.

formulas.name: Mean value of a function

variables.name: mean value
variables.description: The average height of f over the interval.

variables.name: integral of f
variables.description: The definite integral of f from a to b.

formulas.explanation: The mean value is the height of the rectangle on [a, b] that has the same area as the region under f. So it is the integral divided by the width of the interval. It is the continuous version of adding up values and dividing by how many there are.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for average temperature over a day, average velocity from a velocity graph, or average power in a circuit.

example.story: Find the mean value of f(x) = x² on [0, 3]. The integral is 9.

formulas.name: Area between two curves

variables.name: enclosed area
variables.description: Area between the curves from a to b.

variables.name: integral of the upper curve
variables.description: Integral of f (the curve on top) from a to b.

variables.name: integral of the lower curve
variables.description: Integral of g (the curve below) from a to b.

formulas.explanation: The area between two curves is the area under the top one minus the area under the bottom one. Equivalently, integrate the vertical gap f(x) - g(x). The limits are usually the x values where the curves meet.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for regions bounded by two graphs, such as between a line and a parabola.
assumptions: f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b]; otherwise split the interval where they cross

example.story: Find the area enclosed between y = x and y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1, where they meet.
steps: Integral of x from 0 to 1: ½
Integral of x² from 0 to 1: ⅓

formulas.name: Volume of revolution (disc method)

variables.name: volume
variables.description: Volume of the solid made by spinning the curve around the x axis.

variables.name: integral of y²
variables.description: The integral of y² from a to b.

formulas.explanation: Spinning a curve y = f(x) around the x axis makes a solid whose slices are thin discs of radius y and thickness dx. Each disc has volume πy² dx, and adding them up with an integral gives π times the integral of y².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the volume of vases, bowls, nose cones and any shape with circular cross-sections around an axis.
assumptions: for rotation about the y axis use x² and dy instead

example.story: The curve y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 (in metres) is spun around the x axis to make a bowl shape. The integral of y² = x from 0 to 4 is 8 m³.
steps: y² = x, and the integral of x from 0 to 4 is 8

formulas.name: Arc length of a curve (element)

variables.name: length of a short piece
variables.description: Length of the curve over a small step Δx.

variables.name: gradient
variables.description: The slope dy/dx of the curve over that step.

formulas.explanation: Over a small step Δx, a curve with slope m rises by mΔx, so the little piece of curve is a hypotenuse of length √(Δx² + (mΔx)²) = Δx √(1 + m²). Adding up all such pieces, and letting the steps shrink, gives the arc length integral L = ∫√(1 + y'²) dx.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate the length of a curve piece by piece, or as the starting point for setting up an arc length integral.
assumptions: Δx small enough that the slope is nearly constant over the step

example.story: Over a step of 0.1 m, a curve has slope 2. How long is that piece of curve?

formulas.name: Second-order Taylor approximation

variables.name: f(a)
variables.description: Value of the function at the known point a.

variables.name: step
variables.description: Distance x - a from the known point.

formulas.explanation: Near a point a, a smooth function looks like its tangent line, and adding a curvature term makes the match better. The quadratic P matches the function's value, slope and curvature at a. The error shrinks like h³ for small steps.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate function values near a known point, and in physics to approximate potentials near equilibrium.

example.story: Estimate √4.1 using f(x) = √x at a = 4: f(4) = 2, f'(4) = 1/4 and f''(4) = -1/32.

formulas.name: Taylor series term

variables.name: nth term
variables.description: The term of order n in the Taylor series.

variables.name: nth derivative at a
variables.description: The n-th derivative of f at the expansion point a.

variables.name: step
variables.description: Distance x - a from the expansion point.

formulas.explanation: A Taylor series rebuilds a smooth function from its derivatives at one point. The n-th term is the n-th derivative times hⁿ divided by n!. The factorial makes the terms shrink quickly, which is why a few terms often give an excellent approximation. Expanding about a = 0 gives a Maclaurin series.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to approximate functions by polynomials, to estimate errors, and to see which terms matter for small h.
assumptions: f is infinitely differentiable near a
the series converges for this h

example.story: In the series for eˣ about 0 every derivative is 1. What is the n = 4 term for x = 1?

formulas.name: Linear approximation (tangent line)

variables.name: f(a)
variables.description: Value at the known point a.

variables.name: known point
variables.description: Where f and f' are known.

formulas.explanation: Close to a point, a smooth curve is almost straight, so its tangent line gives a good estimate. Start at f(a) and move along the tangent with slope f'(a). The closer x is to a, the better the estimate.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for quick estimates, error propagation, and small-change problems such as how much a volume changes when a radius grows slightly.

example.story: Estimate ln 1.1 using the tangent to ln x at a = 1, where ln 1 = 0 and the gradient is 1.

formulas.name: Maclaurin series for eˣ (cubic)

variables.name: approximation of eˣ
variables.description: Value of the cubic Taylor polynomial.

formulas.explanation: Every derivative of eˣ is eˣ, which equals 1 at x = 0. So the Maclaurin series is 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ..., and the first four terms already give a good approximation for small x. Adding more terms makes it exact in the limit for every x.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to approximate eˣ for small x, or to understand why e^x ≈ 1 + x when x is tiny.
assumptions: |x| small for good accuracy with only four terms

example.story: Estimate e^0.5 with the cubic Maclaurin polynomial.

formulas.name: Maclaurin series for sin x (fifth order)

variables.name: angle
variables.description: The angle in radians, best for small |x|.

formulas.explanation: The derivatives of sin x at 0 cycle through 0, 1, 0, -1, so only odd powers appear, with alternating signs. Keeping just the first term gives the small-angle approximation sin x ≈ x used for pendulums. Calculators use refinements of this idea.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to approximate sin x for small angles, or to justify the small-angle approximation in physics.

example.story: Estimate sin 0.5 with the fifth-order Maclaurin polynomial.

formulas.name: Newton-Raphson step

variables.name: improved estimate
variables.description: The next approximation of the root.

variables.name: current estimate
variables.description: The current approximation of the root.

variables.name: f(x₀)
variables.description: Function value at the current estimate.

variables.name: f'(x₀)
variables.description: Derivative at the current estimate (not zero).

formulas.explanation: Newton's method finds where f(x) = 0 by following the tangent line at the current guess down to the x axis. The tangent hits zero at x₀ - f(x₀)/f'(x₀), which becomes the next guess. Near a simple root the number of correct digits roughly doubles with every step.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to solve equations that have no algebraic solution, or to compute square roots and other values to high precision.
assumptions: the starting guess is close enough to the root

example.story: Improve the guess 1.5 for √2 using f(x) = x² - 2: f(1.5) = 0.25 and f'(1.5) = 3.

formulas.name: Limit of compounding (e to the rt)

variables.name: growth factor
variables.description: How many times bigger the amount becomes.

variables.name: rate
variables.description: Nominal rate per period, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: Compounding n times per period multiplies by (1 + r/n)^(nt). As n grows the factor increases but approaches a limit: e^(rt). This limit is one way to define the number e = lim (1 + 1/n)ⁿ ≈ 2.71828.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to see the upper bound of frequent compounding and as the link between discrete and continuous growth.

example.story: What growth factor does a 5 % rate give over 10 periods with continuous compounding?

formulas.name: Trapezium rule
formulas.explanation: Split the area into n vertical strips of width h and replace the curve on each strip by a straight line, making trapeziums. Each inner y value is shared by two trapeziums, so it counts twice. The rule overestimates for curves that bend upwards and underestimates for curves that bend downwards.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate integrals from data tables or functions that cannot be integrated exactly.

example.story: Estimate the integral of x² from 0 to 1 with two strips (h = 0.5): y₀ = 0, y₁ = 0.25, y₂ = 1.

formulas.name: Simpson's rule (two strips)
formulas.explanation: Simpson's rule fits a parabola through three equally spaced points and integrates it exactly. The weights 1, 4, 1 give the middle point most influence. It is exact for cubics and much more accurate than the trapezium rule for smooth functions. For more strips, repeat the pattern 1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 2, 4, 1.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for accurate numerical integration of smooth functions or evenly spaced data.
assumptions: an even number of strips when extended

example.story: Estimate the integral of x³ from 0 to 2 with h = 1: y₀ = 0, y₁ = 1, y₂ = 8.
steps: I ≈ 1/3 × 12 = 4 (exact, because the curve is a cubic)

formulas.name: Difference quotient (forward difference)

variables.name: f(x + h)
variables.description: Function value a small step to the right.

formulas.explanation: The derivative is defined as the limit of this quotient as h shrinks to zero: the gradient of a chord that slowly turns into the tangent. With a small but finite h it gives a numerical estimate whose error is roughly proportional to h.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate a derivative from data, or to understand differentiation from first principles.
assumptions: h small but not so small that rounding errors dominate

example.story: Estimate the gradient of x² at x = 3 with h = 0.01: f(3.01) = 9.0601 and f(3) = 9.

formulas.name: Central difference

variables.name: f(x + h)
variables.description: Function value a step to the right.

variables.name: f(x - h)
variables.description: Function value a step to the left.

formulas.explanation: Using points on both sides of x makes the chord symmetric about x, so the leading error terms cancel. The error is roughly proportional to h² instead of h, which makes it much more accurate than the forward difference for the same step. For a quadratic it is exact.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for numerical derivatives from evenly spaced data, such as velocity from position measurements.
assumptions: values available on both sides of x

example.story: Estimate the gradient of x² at x = 3 with h = 0.01: f(3.01) = 9.0601 and f(2.99) = 8.9401.
